title: Weather and seasons
goal: Talk about the weather — the safest topic in Estonia — and use verbs that **have no subject at all**, just like English "it's raining".
bekal: describe today's weather and read a simple forecast
name the four seasons and say something happens in that season

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Esimene lumi
dialogs.intro: Mid-November, morning. Kerli knocks on Budi's door.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ma... ma ei ole kunagi lund näinud.
lines.literal: I... I not am ever snow-part seen.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Indoneesias ei saja kunagi lund. Meil on ainult vihm.
lines.id: It never snows in Indonesia. All we have is rain.
lines.literal: Indonesia-in not falls ever snow-part. we-at is only rain.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: How many degrees is it outside?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Umbes miinus kaks. See on soe.
lines.literal: about minus two. that is-it warm.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Jaanuaris on miinus viisteist. Siis on külm.
lines.id: In January it's minus fifteen. That's cold.
lines.literal: January-in is minus fifteen. then is cold.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I need to sit down first.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.id: Don't worry. You'll get used to it.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Kõik harjuvad. Ja kevad tuleb alati.
lines.id: Everyone gets used to it. And spring always comes.
lines.literal: everyone get-used-they. and spring comes-it always.

notes: ⚠️ **Sajab has no subject.** There's no "it" doing the raining; the verb stands alone. Many languages do this — Spanish *llueve*, Italian *piove*, Indonesian *hujan* — while English has to add an *it* that refers to nothing.
**Sajab lund, sajab vihma.** What falls is in the **partitive**, because nobody counts all the snow or all the rain at once. The rule from unit 13 at work again.
**Lähme õue** — "let's go outside". *Õue* is the short illative of *õu* (yard), like *kööki* and *poodi* in unit 7. Its opposite is *tuppa* (indoors).

⚠️ **Minus two counts as warm.** That's not a joke. The Estonian winter hovers between zero and minus five for most of the time, with weeks dipping to minus twenty. Zero degrees in February feels like a real relief.

grammars.title: Verbs without a subject
body: A small group of Estonian verbs talks about weather and time without saying who does it. English has the same group (with a dummy "it"), so this section needs no new way of thinking.
after: The last two rows use the pattern **läheb + adjective + -ks**, meaning "becomes". The pattern is productive: *läheb külmaks* (getting cold), *läheb hiljaks* (getting late), *läheb paremaks* (getting better).
For things that need a subject, Estonian still uses one: *päike paistab* (the sun shines), *tuul puhub* (the wind blows), *lumi sulab* (the snow melts).
⚠️ Notice that the form is always the same as the "he/she" form (*-b*). If you can conjugate verbs from unit 10, you can already build every weather sentence.

grammars.title: The four seasons
body: Seasons take the ending **-l** — the same "surface" set as days and parts of the day.
after: ⚠️ *Suvi* becomes *suvel*, not "suvil" — its genitive is *suve*. Once again it's the noun pairs from unit 6 that decide.
To say "every summer", use *suviti*, like *esmaspäeviti* in unit 9.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice *kümme kraadi **sooja*** and *kümme kraadi **külma*** — Estonian adds "warm" or "cold" instead of plus and minus signs. In written forecasts you'll see *+10* and *−10*, but in conversation people say it in words.

blocks.title: Weather is a safe topic
items: Estonians don't make much small talk, but weather is an exception everyone accepts.
*Küll on täna ilus ilm!* — What lovely weather today!

sections.title: The four seasons, as they really feel

head: Season
Usual temperature
Daylight
What you need to know
rows: Melting snow turns to mud. April is often still snowy.
⚠️ Peaks can reach +30. Most homes have no air conditioning.
The wettest months. The wind bites harder than the temperature.
December is darkest, February is coldest.

blocks.title: Weather words you'll hear
items: ⚠️ *Porilumi* — the mix of snow and mud on March streets. English has no neat equivalent, and Estonians talk about it in the tone others reserve for floods.
